David Hilton alleged in 2014 that Fouche faked one or more of his own military documents and then sought his records under FOIA; the only opened description of Hilton's video of an alleged admission is Johnson's, who says he could not verify it.
Kloor reported that Elizondo's 2016 evaluation rated him exemplary and that Elizondo described his AATIP role as keeping foreign adversaries from penetrating the programme.

contested.text: Mahood's own work concedes ground: he calls Lazar amazingly believable, says he first found the story plausible, and accepts that Lazar's W-2 could be legitimate.
Lazar's friend Gene Huff replied in 1995 that the Pacifica entry was the probation officer's misreading of correspondence courses; the board carries the rebuttal without adopting it.

Johnson reads the FOIA return on Fouche as corroborating what Fouche had said; the decorations in Fouche's own compilation document service as an F-16 avionics NCO and a Strategic Air Command liaison officer.

A podcast claim that Menzel had a thirty-year NSA association and a CIA clearance, said to come from his Harvard papers, would cut against his independence as a sceptic; the board has not reached those papers.

The Condon study that praised Menzel's book was run under an Air Force contract whose sponsor wrote in January 1967 that another study would be needed to see if the Air Force could get out from under the programme.

lead.text: The sceptics' case is carried here as the sceptics made it, with their dated work and its limits: the Harvard astronomer Donald Menzel's books against the extraterrestrial hypothesis, the aviation journalist Philip Klass's newsletter, and Tom Mahood's documentary investigation of Bob Lazar are the core of it.

questions: What do Menzel's Harvard papers actually show about any government ties, and did he make government-funded trips to New Mexico in 1947 and 1948?
What does the National Personnel Records Center file Klass describes show when opened as a document?
Did Fouche ever deliver his 1998 script from a podium? The contemporaneous programme does not list him.
What does the FOIA return on Fouche's records show, and where did Hilton post it?
When were most of Mahood's Lazar pages written, and have any been revised?

record.text: The Condon Report's bibliography lists Menzel's 1953 book and his 1964 paper on whether flying saucers move in straight lines, which the report records as the criticism that set off the orthoteny controversy.

Klass printed the FAA's 1987 press release on JAL flight 1628, which found that a second radar target was an uncorrelated primary and beacon return rather than another aircraft and closed the investigation.

Klass supplied the count behind the Disclosure Project's podium: Greer's book carries taped interviews with 69 witnesses, 20 of whom spoke briefly at the press conference. He also said the witness's claims could have been checked against the National Personnel Records Center.
Klass stated his own limitation: he did not try to attend the 2001 press conference because Greer had refused him before, so his review rests largely on Greer's press releases and book.

The court record Mahood made openable shows that in his 1990 pre-sentence report Lazar listed degrees from Pacifica University, MIT and Caltech; the documents record what he told the court about himself.
The 1982 Los Alamos Monitor article, which Mahood holds, describes Lazar in its own voice as a physicist at the Los Alamos Meson Physics Facility.

Kloor obtained and published the DoD statement of 1 June 2019 that Elizondo had no AATIP responsibilities; the MoD's publication scheme records the Condign executive summary that Clarke's request brought out as released proactively on 15 May 2006.

Check The Evidence, a site run by Andrew Johnson, who signs and dates his posts, is the custodian of Edgar Fouche's 1998 presentation transcript and his self-published military documents; the transcript's own header misspells both IUFOR and Rothshild.

Fouche's own compilation carries its own warnings: the document captioned as a SAC/DARPA classified document carries no classification marking, one commentary passage is signed by Fouche himself, and its last pages turn to arguing against Lazar.

summary.text: Menzel, director of the Harvard College Observatory, published Flying Saucers in 1953, which the Condon Report's history chapter called an excellent book generally regarded as debunking, and his last such book appeared in 1977, a year after his death.

Klass edited the Skeptics UFO Newsletter, which critiqued the Disclosure Project by name within weeks of its May 2001 press conference and published a claimant's service record he had obtained himself.

Mahood, a former civil and traffic engineer with a master's degree in physics, investigated Lazar's credentials and holds the openable copies of the 1982 Los Alamos Monitor article and of the 1990 court material.

Others on the board's sceptical shelf are record-getters rather than debunkers: David Clarke, who wrote the guide to every National Archives UFO tranche, and the journalist Keith Kloor, who obtained a Pentagon denial of Luis Elizondo's role.
